country.name: Romania
country.tagline: Europe's sixth vineyard, ringed by the Carpathians: Fetească in three colours, botrytised Grasă at Cotnari and the Black Sea warmth of Murfatlar.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025: 187 kha of vineyard (all grape uses), 3.3 mhl produced in 2025 (13th in the production table), 17.6% below the five-year average. Eurostat counts 162 kha of wine-grape vines for 2025.

country.overview:
Romania has the biggest vineyard in Central and Eastern Europe: about 187,000 ha in 2025 according to the OIV, the fourth largest in the EU after Spain, France and Italy. In 2025 it made 3.3 million hl of wine, a small crop by its own standards after spring frosts, hail and drought in the west. The shape of the country explains its wine. The Carpathian arc curls through the middle like a horseshoe, and almost every important vineyard sits on its outer or inner foothills: the long eastern and southern flanks in Moldavia and Muntenia, the Transylvanian plateau inside the arc, and the western hills facing Hungary and Serbia. Beyond the mountains lie the Danube terraces, sandy southern plains, and Dobrogea between the Danube and the Black Sea.

The law groups this into eight viticultural regions and, under the EU system, 33 DOCs (*denumire de origine controlată*, PDO) and 12 IGs (PGI). The DOCs range from big hill districts such as Dealu Mare, Târnave, Odobești and Panciu to tiny ones like Pietroasa, Adamclisi and Însurăței. DOC wines can carry a ripeness level: DOC-CMD (harvested at full maturity), DOC-CT (late harvest) and DOC-CIB (noble-berry selection, botrytised).

The native grapes are the reason to explore. Fetească Neagră ('black maiden') is the country's signature red, plummy and spicy, at its best in Dealu Mare. Fetească Albă and Fetească Regală, the latter a natural cross that appeared in Transylvania around 1920, are the main whites. Tămâioasă Românească (a Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains) and the pink-skinned Busuioacă de Bohotin make aromatic dry and sweet wines. Grasă de Cotnari, the same grape as Tokaj's Kövérszőlő, makes botrytised sweet wines at Cotnari that rivalled Tokaji in the 19th century. Băbească Neagră, Negru de Drăgășani, Novac, Crâmpoșie Selecționată, Galbenă de Odobești, Frâncușă and Șarba fill in the local map.

History has whipsawed the industry. Strabo wrote that the Dacian king Burebista ordered vines destroyed; medieval princes such as Stephen the Great endowed monasteries and vineyards; phylloxera, first found at Chitorani in Dealu Mare in the 1880s, forced replanting with French varieties; and the Communist state turned Romania into a bulk supplier for the Soviet bloc, with 80 to 90 percent of output exported in some periods. Since 1989, and especially since EU entry in 2007, investment from Romanian entrepreneurs and foreign partners has modernised wineries such as Cramele Recaș, Jidvei, Prince Știrbey, Davino, LacertA, Avincis, Crama Oprișor, Liliac, Corcova and Bauer. A large share of production is still semi-sweet and sold domestically, but the best dry wines, especially Fetească Neagră and the aromatic whites, are well worth finding.

history.title: Burebista's vine purge
history.text: The Greek geographer Strabo wrote that Burebista, king of the Dacians, on the advice of the priest Decaeneus, ordered vineyards destroyed to keep his warriors sober. Romanian historians regard the passage as exaggerated, but it is the oldest anecdote about wine in the region.

history.title: Greek colonies on the Black Sea
history.text: Greek colonies at Histria, Tomis (Constanța) and Callatis (Mangalia) traded wine and planted vines in Dobrogea, the start of the Murfatlar tradition.

history.title: Roman Dacia
history.text: After Trajan's conquest Roman colonists spread viticulture across Transylvania and Oltenia; the Tropaeum Traiani monument at Adamclisi commemorates the conquest.

history.title: Stephen the Great and Cotnari
history.text: The Moldavian prince Stephen the Great expanded the Cotnari vineyards and court cellars; Grasă de Cotnari has been grown there since his reign.

history.title: Despot Vodă's Latin school
history.text: Prince Despot Vodă founded a Latin school (Schola Latina) at Cotnari in 1562, a sign of the town's wealth from wine; Cotnari reached its peak under him and Stephen the Great.

history.title: Phylloxera at Chitorani
history.text: Phylloxera was first recorded in Romania at Chitorani in Dealu Mare and devastated local viticulture over the following years; replanting through the early 20th century used grafted French varieties.

history.title: Research and Fetească Regală
history.text: The research station at Valea Călugărească and the discovery of Fetească Regală at Daneș in Transylvania around 1920 shaped modern Romanian vine growing.

history.title: State farms and export
history.text: Communist central planning merged estates into state farms (IAS) and cooperatives; up to 80 to 90 percent of wine was exported, much of it to the Soviet Union.

history.title: Privatisation and EU entry
history.text: Land restitution fragmented vineyards; foreign and domestic investors rebuilt wineries, and Romania joined the EU in 2007, registering its DOCs the same year.

country.classification:
Romanian wine law follows the EU: 33 DOCs (*denumire de origine controlată*, the Romanian name for a PDO) and 12 IGs (*indicație geografică*, PGI), plus wine without origin. Several DOCs list sub-denominations that can appear on labels (for example Dealu Mare-Urlați, Dealu Mare-Valea Călugărească, Murfatlar-Medgidia, Târnave-Jidvei). DOC wines may also carry a ripeness level:
- DOC-CMD (*cules la maturitate deplină*): full ripeness, at least 187 g/l of sugar at harvest
- DOC-CT (*cules târziu*): late harvest, at least 220 g/l
- DOC-CIB (*cules la înnobilarea boabelor*): botrytised berry selection, at least 240 g/l

The national body ONVPV (Oficiul Național al Viei și Produselor Vitivinicole) manages registration and control. Adamclisi (2020) and Însurăței (2018) are the newest DOCs.
country.climate_soils: The climate is continental, with hot summers and cold winters; the Carpathians shelter the eastern and southern foothills from cold air, and the Black Sea moderates Dobrogea, the sunniest and driest part of the country. Soils range from the chernozem and loess-covered hills of Moldavia and Muntenia, the marls and clays of Transylvania and the limestone and loess of Dobrogea to the sand dunes of Oltenia's southern plain (Sadova-Corabia).

grapes.name: Fetească Neagră
grapes.note: The signature native red: plum, black cherry and spice; best in Dealu Mare, Dobrogea and Moldavia.

grapes.name: Fetească Regală
grapes.note: The most planted native white, a natural cross of Fetească Albă and Frâncușă first noted at Daneș around 1920; crisp, floral, often sparkling.

grapes.name: Fetească Albă
grapes.note: Old Moldavian and Transylvanian white, softer and more aromatic.

grapes.name: Tămâioasă Românească
grapes.note: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, famous for sweet wines at Pietroasa and Cotnari.

grapes.name: Grasă de Cotnari
grapes.note: Botrytis-prone white, identical to Tokaj's Kövérszőlő; sweet wines with up to about 300 g/l of sugar.

grapes.name: Băbească Neagră
grapes.note: Light, sour-cherry red of southern Moldavia (Nicorești, Dealu Bujorului).

grapes.name: Busuioacă de Bohotin
grapes.note: Pink-skinned Muscat with basil-like aromatics, from Bohotin near Iași.

grapes.name: Crâmpoșie Selecționată
grapes.note: Crisp white of Drăgășani, a selection of the old Crâmpoșie.

grapes.name: Negru de Drăgășani and Novac
grapes.note: Red crossings bred at Drăgășani in the 1990s from local and international parents.

grapes.name: Galbenă de Odobești, Frâncușă, Șarba
grapes.note: Local whites of Vrancea and Moldavia; Șarba is aromatic, Galbenă tart.

regions.name: Moldavian Hills
regions.tagline: Romania's largest wine region, from noble-rot Cotnari to the vast Vrancea vineyards.
regions.summary: The Moldavian Hills (Dealurile Moldovei) cover eastern Romania between the Carpathians and the Prut, roughly a third of the country's vineyard. In the north, around Iași, lie Cotnari, Iași, Bohotin, Huși and Iana; in the south the huge Vrancea block of Panciu, Odobești and Cotești, one of the largest continuous vineyards in Europe, and Nicorești and Dealu Bujorului in Galați county. Whites dominate: Fetească Albă and Regală, Grasă, Tămâioasă, Frâncușă, Șarba and Galbenă de Odobești, with Băbească Neagră and Fetească Neagră as the reds.
regions.history: The medieval princes of Moldavia, Stephen the Great above all, made Cotnari's wine a court drink; monasteries owned large estates. Under Communism Vrancea and Huși became bulk wine centres, and Huși was linked to Nicolae Ceaușescu's favourite wines.
regions.terroir: Loess, clay and sandstone hills, continental climate with cold winters; Cotnari's autumn fogs favour botrytis.
regions.grapes: Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Grasă de Cotnari, Tămâioasă Românească, Frâncușă, Busuioacă de Bohotin, Șarba, Zghihară de Huși, Galbenă de Odobești, Băbească Neagră, Fetească Neagră.
regions.styles: Sweet and semi-sweet aromatic whites, crisp dry whites, sparkling (Panciu), light reds.
regions.classification: DOCs Cotnari, Iași, Bohotin, Huși, Iana, Panciu, Odobești, Cotești, Nicorești, Dealu Bujorului; IG Dealurile Moldovei.

regions.name: Muntenia and Oltenia Hills
regions.tagline: The southern Carpathian foothills: Dealu Mare's Fetească Neagră and Drăgășani's crisp whites.
regions.summary: The southern face of the Carpathians, from Buzău and Prahova in the east to Mehedinți in the west, is Romania's red-wine heartland. Dealu Mare ('big hill') is the leading DOC, a 65 km south-facing ridge with Urlați, Valea Călugărească, Ceptura and Merei; Pietroasa at its eastern end is famed for sweet Tămâioasă. West of the Olt, Oltenia has Drăgășani (Crâmpoșie, Negru de Drăgășani, Novac), Sâmburești, Ștefănești, Banu Mărăcine near Craiova, Segarcea (once the royal crown estate) and Mehedinți near the Iron Gates.
regions.history: Dealu Mare was the scene of phylloxera's first Romanian outbreak at Chitorani. Valea Călugărească ('valley of the monks') hosted the national research institute. Segarcea was a royal domain from 1884 to 1948. Prince Știrbey's family estate at Drăgășani was restituted in 2001 and revived.
regions.terroir: South-facing slopes on clay, loess and marls; warm summers and good autumn sunshine ripen red grapes reliably.
regions.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Negru de Drăgășani, Novac, Tămâioasă Românească, Crâmpoșie Selecționată, Fetească Regală, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Full-bodied reds, aromatic sweet wines (Pietroasa), crisp whites (Drăgășani).
regions.classification: DOCs Dealu Mare, Pietroasa, Drăgășani, Sâmburești, Ștefănești, Banu Mărăcine, Segarcea, Mehedinți; IG Dealurile Munteniei, Dealurile Olteniei.

regions.name: Transylvanian Plateau
regions.tagline: Saxon villages, fortified churches and cool, crisp whites inside the Carpathian arc.
regions.summary: Inside the Carpathian arc, the Transylvanian Plateau sits at 300 to 500 m with a cool continental climate. Its DOCs are Târnave (the valleys of the Târnava Mare and Mică, home of Jidvei, Romania's largest single estate), Alba Iulia, Aiud, Sebeș-Apold and Lechința. The wines are aromatic, high-acid whites: Fetească Regală (discovered at Daneș near Sighișoara), Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris, and traditional-method sparkling.
regions.history: Transylvanian Saxons, German settlers invited by Hungarian kings from the 12th century, built fortified churches in wine villages such as Biertan, Apold and Mediaș; their cellars and vineyards were abandoned after their emigration in 1990, and revival has been slow but real.
regions.terroir: Marl and clay hills, cooler and wetter than the rest of Romania, with a late harvest and high acidity.
regions.grapes: Fetească Regală, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer Roz, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Neuburger, Iordana.
regions.styles: Crisp dry and off-dry whites, sparkling, some Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: DOCs Târnave, Alba Iulia, Aiud, Sebeș-Apold, Lechința; IG Dealurile Transilvaniei.

regions.name: Dobrogea
regions.tagline: Between the Danube and the Black Sea: Romania's sunniest, driest vineyards.
regions.summary: Dobrogea, the land between the lower Danube and the Black Sea, is Romania's sunniest region, with more than 300 sunny days in places and very low rainfall. Murfatlar, near Constanța, is its most famous DOC, known for rich, often sweet, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Muscat Ottonel as well as Fetească Neagră reds. Other DOCs are Oltina and Adamclisi in the south-west, and Babadag and Sarica Niculițel in the north, around the old Hercynian Măcin hills near the Danube Delta.
regions.history: Greek colonies (Histria, Tomis, Callatis) traded wine; the Romans fought for this frontier, leaving Tropaeum Traiani at Adamclisi. Niculițel has a 4th-century Christian martyrs' basilica. Murfatlar's research station and large state winery made it a household name.
regions.terroir: Limestone and loess plateaus, chalky soils at Murfatlar, very warm dry summers; the Black Sea moderates winter.
regions.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Muscat Ottonel, Tămâioasă Românească, Columna.
regions.styles: Ripe reds, rich whites, sweet late-harvest wines.
regions.classification: DOCs Murfatlar, Oltina, Adamclisi, Babadag, Sarica Niculițel; IG Dealurile Dobrogei.

regions.name: Banat
regions.tagline: The south-west: Recaș's big modern winery and Serbian-influenced vineyards on the Danube.
regions.summary: The Banat region in south-western Romania borders Serbia and Hungary. Its DOCs are Recaș, built around one of Romania's largest and most modern wineries, and Banat, covering the Moldova Nouă and Dealurile Tirolului areas near the Danube. Cadarcă (Kadarka), Burgund Mare (Blaufränkisch) and Riesling are traditional here; international varieties now dominate.
regions.history: Banat was Habsburg land after 1718, settled by Swabians, Serbs, Romanians and Czechs; Recaș's vineyards date from the 15th century, and the modern winery was rebuilt after 1998 by Romanian and British partners.
regions.terroir: Clay and sandy loams, warm with a sub-Mediterranean touch.
regions.grapes: Cadarcă, Burgund Mare, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Modern varietal reds and whites, sparkling.
regions.classification: DOCs Recaș and Banat; IG Viile Timișului.

regions.name: Crișana and Maramureș
regions.tagline: The western hills toward Hungary: Miniș's Cadarcă and Crișana's white wines.
regions.summary: The western hills of Crișana and Maramureș face the Pannonian plain. Miniș, in the Zărand hills near Arad, is known for Cadarcă red and the local white Mustoasă de Măderat; Crișana, around Oradea and Zalău, makes mostly whites.
regions.history: Miniș is one of the oldest documented vineyard areas in Romania; the region shares Hungarian and Habsburg history with the Carpathian Basin.
regions.terroir: Volcanic and marl slopes in the Zărand hills, clays and sands in Crișana.
regions.grapes: Cadarcă, Burgund Mare, Fetească Neagră, Mustoasă de Măderat, Riesling Italian, Fetească Regală, Furmint.
regions.classification: DOCs Miniș and Crișana; IG Dealurile Zarandului and Dealurile Crișanei.

regions.name: Danube Terraces and Southern Sands
regions.tagline: The Danube floodplain terraces and sand dunes of the south.
regions.summary: The Danube Terraces and the sandy plains of southern Romania (Sadova-Corabia, Calafat, Dăbuleni) are mostly bulk-wine areas covered by IGs such as Dealurile Olteniei and Terasele Dunării. Însurăței, in Brăila county on the Danube's left bank, gained DOC status in 2018 and produces crisp whites and reds from Fetească Neagră, Syrah and Cabernet.
regions.history: Sandy soils resistant to phylloxera made these plains important for ungrafted vineyards in the 20th century.
regions.terroir: Sand dunes and Danube terraces; hot, dry summers.
regions.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian.
regions.classification: DOC Însurăței; IGs Terasele Dunării and others.

ro-adamclisi.name: Adamclisi
ro-adamclisi.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
ro-adamclisi.summary: Adamclisi became Romania's newest DOC in July 2020, a single commune in southern Dobrogea named for the Roman Tropaeum Traiani monument. Its rules allow only six varieties (Fetească Neagră, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc) at a low 7 t/ha. Alira and Viile Metamorfosis' neighbours have planted modern vineyards here.

ro-aiud.name: Aiud
ro-aiud.grapes: Fetească Regală, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer Roz, Iordana
ro-aiud.summary: Aiud, north of Alba Iulia along the Mureș, makes crisp Transylvanian whites from Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer and the local crossing Iordana. Its six communes include Ocna Mureș, a salt-mining town, and the hills are cool enough for good sparkling base wine.

ro-alba-iulia.name: Alba Iulia
ro-alba-iulia.grapes: Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Traminer Roz, Neuburger, Pinot Gris
ro-alba-iulia.summary: Alba Iulia, around the citadel city on the Mureș where the union of Transylvania with Romania was proclaimed in 1918, is a small white-wine DOC of seven communes including Ighiu and Cricău. Riesling Italian, Fetească Regală, Muscat Ottonel and Traminer dominate.

ro-babadag.name: Babadag
ro-babadag.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Băbească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Aligoté, Fetească Regală, Columna
ro-babadag.summary: Babadag, in northern Dobrogea near the Razim-Sinoe lagoons of the Danube Delta and the Greek ruins of Histria, covers 13 communes making whites and reds in a dry, windy climate. Aligoté and the Murfatlar-bred Columna are local specialities.

ro-banat.name: Banat
ro-banat.grapes: Cadarcă, Burgund Mare, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Riesling Italian, Fetească Regală, Majarcă Albă
ro-banat.summary: The Banat DOC covers the hills of Moldova Nouă and the Dealurile Tirolului near the Danube gorge and the Serbian border. It makes both reds and whites; the area's Czech-founded villages and Danube landscapes give it character.

ro-banu-maracine.name: Banu Mărăcine
ro-banu-maracine.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Novac, Tămâioasă Românească, Fetească Regală
ro-banu-maracine.summary: Banu Mărăcine is a small DOC around Craiova named after the University of Craiova's teaching and research station; it produces reds and whites from Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet and Tămâioasă.

ro-bohotin.name: Bohotin
ro-bohotin.grapes: Busuioacă de Bohotin, Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Aligoté
ro-bohotin.summary: Bohotin, south-east of Iași near the Prut, gives its name to Busuioacă de Bohotin, a pink-skinned muscat with a basil-like perfume (*busuioc* means basil), made dry or sweet as a dark rosé. The DOC covers six communes.

ro-cotesti.name: Cotești
ro-cotesti.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Băbească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian
ro-cotesti.summary: Cotești, in southern Vrancea, makes both whites and the region's best-known reds (Fetească Neagră, Băbească Neagră, Merlot) on warmer south-facing slopes; it has high permitted yields and is largely a volume area.

ro-cotnari.name: Cotnari
ro-cotnari.grapes: Grasă de Cotnari, Fetească Albă, Tămâioasă Românească, Frâncușă, Busuioacă de Bohotin
ro-cotnari.summary: Cotnari, in the hills north-west of Iași, is Romania's most famous historic wine and its answer to Tokaj. The DOC (nine communes) is dedicated to four local whites: Grasă de Cotnari, Fetească Albă, Tămâioasă Românească and Frâncușă, plus the pink Busuioacă de Bohotin. Autumn fogs bring noble rot to Grasă, the same grape as Tokaj's Kövérszőlő, and the best wines are sweet, honeyed and long-lived; residual sugar of about 300 g/l is common, and the 1958 harvest reached about 520 g/l. The vineyards are documented since the 15th century and reached their peak under Peter II, Stephen the Great (1457 to 1504) and Despot Vodă, who founded a Latin school at Cotnari in 1562. The large Cotnari company, privatised after 1989, is one of Romania's biggest single estates, and Casa de Vinuri Cotnari makes dry versions of the same grapes.
ro-cotnari.terroir: Clay and sandy loams on the Cotnari hills at 150 to 400 m; autumn fogs encourage botrytis; continental climate with harsh winters.
ro-cotnari.nerd_note: Cotnari's Grasă and Tokaj's Kövérszőlő are the same variety: two historic sweet-wine regions on either side of the Carpathians share a grape.

ro-crisana.name: Crișana
ro-crisana.grapes: Fetească Regală, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Mustoasă de Măderat, Pinot Gris, Fetească Neagră
ro-crisana.summary: Crișana covers the north-western hills around Oradea, Diosig, Șimleu Silvaniei and Zalău (23 communes), close to the Hungarian border, making mostly whites from Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian and Mustoasă de Măderat, with some Fetească Neagră.

ro-dealu-bujorului.name: Dealu Bujorului
ro-dealu-bujorului.grapes: Băbească Neagră, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Fetească Albă, Aligoté
ro-dealu-bujorului.summary: Dealu Bujorului ('peony hill') around Târgu Bujor in Galați county is a warm, southern Moldavian DOC with a research station; it makes reds (Băbească Neagră, Fetească Neagră, Merlot) and whites.

ro-dealu-mare.name: Dealu Mare
ro-dealu-mare.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Tămâioasă Românească
ro-dealu-mare.summary: Dealu Mare ('the big hill') is Romania's leading red-wine DOC: a 65 km band of south-facing foothills from Buzău to Ploiești, with 18 to 20 communes including Urlați, Ceptura, Valea Călugărească, Breaza, Merei and Năeni. Sheltered by the Carpathians and open to the southern sun, it ripens Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir into rich, plush reds, and its eastern end produces aromatic sweet Tămâioasă. It was where phylloxera first appeared in Romania, at Chitorani, and it is now the base of many of the country's best modern wineries: Davino, LacertA, Serve, Budureasca, Basilescu, Rotenberg, Aurelia Vișinescu, Crama Gîrboiu's neighbours and the historic Halewood estate. Sub-denominations such as Urlați, Valea Călugărească, Ceptura, Merei, Breaza, Zorești and Tohani can appear on labels.
ro-dealu-mare.terroir: South-facing slopes of 130 to 550 m on clays, marls and loess; warm and sunny, sheltered from northern cold.
ro-dealu-mare.nerd_note: Valea Călugărească ('valley of the monks') houses Romania's national viticulture research institute, which has bred and selected many of the country's clones.

ro-dragasani.name: Drăgășani
ro-dragasani.grapes: Crâmpoșie Selecționată, Tămâioasă Românească, Sauvignon Blanc, Fetească Regală, Negru de Drăgășani, Novac, Fetească Neagră
ro-dragasani.summary: Drăgășani follows the right bank of the Olt in Vâlcea county, a long chain of hills with eleven communes. It is known for crisp, herbal Crâmpoșie Selecționată, aromatic Tămâioasă Românească, Sauvignon Blanc, and two reds bred here, Negru de Drăgășani and Novac. The Știrbey family estate, restituted in 2001 and revived by Ileana Kripp-Costinescu and the Austrian winemaker Oliver Bauer, made the area's modern reputation; Avincis and Bauer are other leading names.
ro-dragasani.nerd_note: Novac and Negru de Drăgășani were both bred at the Drăgășani research station in the 1980s and 1990s by crossing the local Negru Vârtos with Georgia's Saperavi.

ro-husi.name: Huși
ro-husi.grapes: Zghihară de Huși, Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Busuioacă de Bohotin, Aligoté, Fetească Neagră
ro-husi.summary: Huși, near the Prut and the Moldovan border, is famous for Zghihară de Huși, a tart, light local white, and for being a favourite source of wine for the Communist leadership. The DOC covers 17 communes with a long variety list.

ro-iana.name: Iana
ro-iana.grapes: Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Aligoté, Busuioacă de Bohotin, Băbească Neagră
ro-iana.summary: Iana is a small DOC in Vaslui county in central Moldavia (five communes), producing light whites and reds from Fetească Albă, Aligoté, Băbească Neagră and Busuioacă de Bohotin. Most of its wine is sold locally and in bulk; the DOC exists largely to protect a historic name.

ro-iasi.name: Iași
ro-iasi.grapes: Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Aligoté, Busuioacă de Bohotin, Golia, Arcaș, Fetească Neagră
ro-iasi.summary: The Iași DOC surrounds Moldavia's historic capital, with 13 communes on hills such as Copou and Bucium. It makes aromatic whites and some reds, and is home to university research that bred the Golia and Arcaș varieties.

ro-insuratei.name: Însurăței
ro-insuratei.grapes: Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Riesling, Chardonnay, Fetească Neagră, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
ro-insuratei.summary: Însurăței, in Brăila county on the Danube plain, became a DOC in 2018 (four communes). It makes fresh whites and reds from Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Riesling, Chardonnay, Fetească Neagră, Syrah and Cabernet.

ro-lechinta.name: Lechința
ro-lechinta.grapes: Fetească Regală, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Sauvignon Blanc, Traminer Roz, Pinot Noir
ro-lechinta.summary: Lechința, in Bistrița-Năsăud in northern Transylvania, is a cool white-wine DOC of 17 communes; Liliac's modern winery at Batoș has raised its profile with crisp Fetească Regală, Sauvignon and Pinot Noir.

ro-mehedinti.name: Mehedinți
ro-mehedinti.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Novac, Negru de Drăgășani, Tămâioasă Românească
ro-mehedinti.summary: Mehedinți, in the far south-west near the Danube's Iron Gates and Drobeta-Turnu Severin, covers about 20 communes including the Corcova and Oprișor areas. Crama Oprișor and Corcova Roy & Dâmboviceanu make some of Romania's most structured reds here.

ro-minis.name: Miniș
ro-minis.grapes: Cadarcă, Burgund Mare, Fetească Neagră, Mustoasă de Măderat, Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Furmint
ro-minis.summary: Miniș, in the Zărand hills near Arad, is one of Romania's oldest documented vineyard areas, famous for Cadarcă (Kadarka) red and the local white Mustoasă de Măderat; the DOC covers still, semi-sparkling and quality sparkling wine across nine communes.

ro-murfatlar.name: Murfatlar
ro-murfatlar.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Muscat Ottonel, Tămâioasă Românească, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
ro-murfatlar.summary: Murfatlar lies just inland from Constanța on the Black Sea, in Dobrogea's chalky, sun-baked hills; it is one of the sunniest vineyard areas in Europe, with very little rain. The DOC (14 communes, with sub-denominations Medgidia, Cernavodă and Megidia) became famous under Communism for rich, late-harvested, often sweet Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Muscat Ottonel from the big state winery and research station; today the Murfatlar company and smaller estates also make ripe reds from Fetească Neagră, Merlot and Cabernet. The local white crossing Columna was bred at the Murfatlar station.
ro-murfatlar.terroir: Limestone and chalky loess plateaus; very warm and dry, over 300 days of sun, moderated by the Black Sea.

ro-nicoresti.name: Nicorești
ro-nicoresti.grapes: Băbească Neagră, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Fetească Albă
ro-nicoresti.summary: Nicorești, in Galați county, is the classic home of Băbească Neagră, a light, sour-cherry red with bright acidity and low tannin that is best drunk young and cool. The DOC (eight communes) also produces Fetească Neagră and whites.

ro-odobesti.name: Odobești
ro-odobesti.grapes: Galbenă de Odobești, Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Băbească Neagră, Fetească Neagră
ro-odobesti.summary: Odobești, in Vrancea, is one of Romania's oldest and most extensive vineyard areas, on the slopes below the Măgura Odobești. It is known for whites, especially the tart local Galbenă de Odobești, Fetească Albă and Riesling Italian, and large-volume production.

ro-oltina.name: Oltina
ro-oltina.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
ro-oltina.summary: Oltina lies in south-western Dobrogea near the Danube and the Bulgarian border, with seven communes including Aliman and Ostrov making ripe reds and whites in a warm, dry climate. The nearby Danube lakes temper the summer heat a little.

ro-panciu.name: Panciu
ro-panciu.grapes: Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Șarba, Galbenă de Odobești, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
ro-panciu.summary: Panciu, in northern Vrancea, is known for crisp whites and above all for sparkling wine: the DOC covers quality sparkling and aromatic sparkling (Muscat Ottonel, Tămâioasă, Șarba) as well as still wines, and the town's old cellars, rebuilt after the 1940 and 1977 earthquakes, hold millions of bottles. The area was a front line in World War I (Mărășești, 1917).

ro-pietroasa.name: Pietroasa
ro-pietroasa.grapes: Tămâioasă Românească, Grasă de Cotnari, Busuioacă de Bohotin, Fetească Neagră
ro-pietroasa.summary: Pietroasa, a single commune (Pietroasele) at the eastern end of the Dealu Mare hills in Buzău county, is famous for sweet Tămâioasă Românească grown on limestone-rich slopes; the University of Agronomic Sciences in Bucharest runs a research station here. The village is also where the Pietroasa Treasure, a 4th-century Gothic gold hoard, was found in 1837.

ro-recas.name: Recaș
ro-recas.grapes: Fetească Neagră, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Fetească Regală, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
ro-recas.summary: Recaș is a single-commune DOC near Timișoara built around Cramele Recaș, rebuilt from 1998 by Romanian and British partners into one of Romania's largest and most export-focused wineries, with about 1,000 ha. Its vineyards date from the 15th century. It makes everything from inexpensive varietals to the Solo Quinta and Cuvée Uberland ranges, and is the source of much of the Romanian wine seen in UK supermarkets.

ro-samburesti.name: Sâmburești
ro-samburesti.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Fetească Neagră, Novac, Negru de Drăgășani
ro-samburesti.summary: Sâmburești, in Olt county, was a renowned Cabernet Sauvignon estate in the Communist era, when its reds were among Romania's most prestigious; the DOC covers two communes and is still known for Cabernet and Merlot.

ro-sarica-niculitel.name: Sarica Niculițel
ro-sarica-niculitel.grapes: Aligoté, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Fetească Regală, Rkatsiteli
ro-sarica-niculitel.summary: Sarica Niculițel, near Tulcea at the gateway to the Danube Delta, is a hilly DOC of 14 communes on the old Măcin hills, known for Aligoté, Fetească Neagră and Merlot.

ro-sebes-apold.name: Sebeș-Apold
ro-sebes-apold.grapes: Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Iordana
ro-sebes-apold.summary: Sebeș-Apold spans the hills between Sebeș and the Saxon villages of Apold and Gârbova; its 12 communes make fresh whites and some reds, and the area's Saxon fortified churches recall its German past.

ro-segarcea.name: Segarcea
ro-segarcea.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Fetească Neagră, Merlot, Tămâioasă Roză, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
ro-segarcea.summary: Segarcea, south of Craiova, was the Crown Domain (Domeniul Coroanei) of the Romanian royal family from 1884 until 1948; nationalised by the Communists, it was revived in the 2000s and now makes Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Fetească Neagră and Tămâioasă roză.

ro-stefanesti.name: Ștefănești
ro-stefanesti.grapes: Fetească Regală, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Tămâioasă Românească, Burgund Mare, Cabernet Sauvignon
ro-stefanesti.summary: Ștefănești, near Pitești in Argeș county, hosts a long-standing viticulture research station; the DOC (six communes) produces whites and reds from Fetească Regală, Riesling Italian, Tămâioasă and Burgund Mare (Blaufränkisch), with yields capped at 10 t/ha.

ro-tarnave.name: Târnave
ro-tarnave.grapes: Fetească Regală, Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Sauvignon Blanc, Traminer, Pinot Gris
ro-tarnave.summary: Târnave is the largest Transylvanian DOC, covering the valleys of the Târnava Mare and Târnava Mică between Blaj, Mediaș and Sighișoara (about 35 communes). It is cool and high, so the wines are crisp, aromatic whites: Fetească Regală (first noted at Daneș nearby), Fetească Albă, Riesling Italian, Muscat Ottonel, Sauvignon Blanc and Traminer, plus traditional-method sparkling. Jidvei, Romania's largest estate with about 2,500 ha, dominates; its headquarters is the Bethlen-Haller castle at Cetatea de Baltă. Sub-denominations include Jidvei, Mediaș, Blaj, Dealurile Mureșului and Dumbrăveni.
ro-tarnave.terroir: Marl and clay hills at 300 to 500 m; cool continental climate, late harvest, high acidity.

sites.name: Cotnari winery
sites.text: Cotnari's main winery sits below the hill where Stephen the Great kept his court cellars. The company farms one of Romania's largest single vineyards of Grasă, Fetească Albă, Tămâioasă and Frâncușă and keeps a large archive of sweet wines, some decades old.

sites.name: Cotnari, Cătălina hill
sites.text: On Cătălina hill above Cotnari stood a Geto-Dacian fortress about 2,500 years ago; finds suggest viticulture dates to Burebista's time. The town later held one of Moldavia's largest fairs and a Latin school founded by Despot Vodă in 1562.

sites.name: Sarmizegetusa Regia
sites.text: The mountain capital of the Dacian kingdom in the Orăștie Mountains, a UNESCO site. According to Strabo, Burebista and his priest Decaeneus ordered the Dacians' vines destroyed, Europe's earliest recorded anti-wine edict.

sites.name: Tropaeum Traiani, Adamclisi
sites.text: This Roman victory monument was raised in 109 AD to celebrate Trajan's conquest of Dacia. It gives its name to Adamclisi, Romania's newest wine DOC (2020).

sites.name: Bethlen-Haller Castle, Cetatea de Baltă (Jidvei)
sites.text: This Renaissance castle on the Târnava Mică was built for the Bethlen family in the 17th century. It now serves as the headquarters and showpiece of Jidvei, Romania's largest single wine estate, with about 2,500 ha of Transylvanian vineyards.

sites.name: Cramele Recaș
sites.text: Rebuilt after 1998 by Romanian and British partners, Cramele Recaș is one of the largest and most modern wineries in Romania, with about 1,000 ha near Timișoara. Recaș's vineyards date from the 15th century.

sites.name: Prince Știrbey
sites.text: The Știrbey princely family's estate at Drăgășani was nationalised under Communism and restituted in 2001. Ileana Kripp-Costinescu and the Austrian winemaker Oliver Bauer revived it, championing Crâmpoșie Selecționată, Tămâioasă and Novac.

sites.name: LacertA
sites.text: LacertA, named for a protected lizard of the Dealu Mare hills, is a modern estate at Năeni whose Fetească Neagră and Bordeaux blends exemplify the new Dealu Mare.

sites.name: Valea Călugărească
sites.text: The 'Valley of the Monks' in Dealu Mare has long housed Romania's national viticulture research institute. Phylloxera was first recorded nearby at Chitorani in the 1880s, which makes this valley the starting point of modern Romanian vine growing.

sites.name: Pietroasele
sites.text: Pietroasele at the east end of Dealu Mare is famous for sweet Tămâioasă Românească and for the Pietroasa Treasure, a 4th-century Gothic gold hoard found here in 1837.

sites.name: Murfatlar winery
sites.text: Murfatlar's winery and research station near Constanța made the name famous under Communism for rich, late-harvest Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Muscat Ottonel from chalky, sun-baked hills.

sites.name: Domeniul Coroanei Segarcea
sites.text: Segarcea was the Romanian royal family's crown wine domain from 1884. It was nationalised in 1948 and revived as a private estate in the 2000s, making Cabernet Sauvignon and Tămâioasă roză.

sites.name: Panciu
sites.text: Panciu in northern Vrancea is Romania's sparkling-wine town, with cellars holding millions of bottles. It was rebuilt after a 1940 earthquake and lies near the World War I battlefield of Mărășești.

sites.name: Odobești
sites.text: Odobești is the centre of one of the oldest and largest vineyard areas in Romania, on the slopes of the Măgura Odobești in Vrancea, home of the tart local white Galbenă de Odobești.

sites.name: Banu Mărăcine station
sites.text: The University of Craiova's teaching and research vineyard on the city's outskirts gives its name to the small Banu Mărăcine DOC. It is named after a medieval Oltenian boyar, and its vines are used for student training and clonal trials.

sites.name: Crama Oprișor
sites.text: Crama Oprișor at Oprișor in Mehedinți, in Romania's far south-west near the Danube, was one of the first modern estates of the 2000s. It is known for structured Fetească Neagră and Bordeaux blends such as La Cetate, from warm, south-facing slopes.
